## Where we are

- W01: a generative model **produces samples** — and we saw a complete one on two data points
- The loop of this module: **distribution → samples → fitted distribution → new samples**
- Today we make the word **fit** precise: maximum likelihood

::: {.note}
Tomorrow: KL divergence (how wrong is a fit?). Then: empirical risk minimization.
:::

## The cast of distributions

| Family | Support | Knobs | Natural habitat |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{Uniform}(a,b)$ | $[a,b]$ | endpoints | total ignorance on an interval |
| $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | center, width | noise, sums of small effects |
| $\mathrm{Gamma}(k,\theta)$ | $(0,\infty)$ | shape, scale | waiting times, positive skew |
| $\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ | $(0,1)$ | two shapes | proportions, probabilities |
| Mixture | $\mathbb{R}$ | weights + components | multimodal data — clusters |

Five shapes cover most of what this course needs — and the mixture is the star of
the semester.

## What the histogram is telling you

- Density-normalized histogram → as $n$ grows it **hugs the pdf**: samples carry
  the distribution
- $n = 30$ is ragged, $n = 3000$ is faithful — *estimation error shrinks like
  $1/\sqrt{n}$* (Module 1 will say this properly)
- Fitting = choosing the family member that makes the observed samples **most probable**

## PDF vs likelihood — the confusion, dissolved

```{=html}
<iframe src="likelihood-lens.html" style="width:100%;height:70%;border:1px solid #cfdcec;border-radius:8px" loading="lazy" title="Likelihood lens"></iframe>
```

## One function, two readings

$$f(x; \theta)$$

| Fix | Vary | You get | Area under curve |
|---|---|---|---|
| parameters $\theta$ | data $x$ | **pdf** — a distribution over data | $=1$, always |
| observed data $x$ | parameters $\theta$ | **likelihood** — a score for fitting | meaningless |

::: {.note}
The likelihood is **not** a probability distribution over $\theta$. Only its
argmax — and its shape near the argmax — carries information.
:::

## Likelihood of a dataset

Independent observations multiply; logs turn products into sums:

$$L(\theta) = \prod_{i} f(x_i; \theta)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i} \log f(x_i; \theta)$$

- The log changes nothing about *where* the maximum is (log is monotone)
- …and everything about how pleasant the algebra is
- Numerically: products of 3000 small numbers underflow; sums of logs do not

## To the board: the Gaussian MLE

Maximize

$$\ell(\mu,\sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i (x_i-\mu)^2$$

- $\partial\ell/\partial\mu = 0 \implies \hat\mu = \bar x$ (the sample mean — for every $\sigma$)
- $\partial\ell/\partial\sigma^2 = 0 \implies \hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2$

::: {.note}
Derivation on the board now — it is tonight's Exercise if you want to redo it
alone. Note the divisor $n$, not $n-1$: the MLE is (slightly) biased.
:::

## Honesty about the other families

| Family | How we fit it | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | maximum likelihood | closed form — you just derived it |
| Uniform | maximum likelihood | closed form: $\hat a = \min$, $\hat b = \max$ (cute proof — exercise) |
| Gamma | **method of moments** | MLE has *no closed form*: match $\bar x$ and $s^2$ instead |
| Beta | **method of moments** | same story |
| Mixture | …? | stay tuned — this one needs real machinery (EM, later) |

Method of moments: set the family's mean and variance equal to the sample's.
Simple, honest, and a good estimator to know by itself.

## The trap: right method, wrong family

- In the playground: mixture data, 3000 samples, press **Fit**
- The single best Normal — by *maximum likelihood, done perfectly* — puts its peak
  **where the data is emptiest**
- Fitting well within the wrong family is still wrong

::: {.note}
Needed: a way to **measure** the gap between the data distribution and the model.
That measure is KL divergence — tomorrow.
:::
